stop 2 card 13, answer 2: copies a Prep line word for word

explanations.explanation: That's the one. Ruth 1:1 says the family leaves Bethlehem in Judah to go reside in the land of Moab. Not a short trip, either. That's like me hopping off my gold base and rolling all the way to the next planet over.

Egypt's the wrong direction, friend. Egypt shows up plenty in the Bible, but not here. Ruth 1:1 says Moab. Egypt's where Israel was enslaved, where Joseph stored grain, where Jesus' family fled. Different story, different kitchen entirely.

Edom's close geographically but wrong for this passage. Ruth 1:1 says Moab. Edom was Esau's descendants, east of Israel too, but Elimelech's family went to Moab. I know, the names all sound like someone clearing their throat, but the text is clear.
Ruth it is. Ruth 1:4 names her plain as day: Orpah and Ruth. Ruth's the one who sticks. She's the one this whole book is named after. You don't name a book after someone who leaves in chapter one.
Rachel's a famous name, but she's Jacob's wife from way back in Genesis. Ruth 1:4 says Ruth. Rachel's been gone for centuries by this point. Wrong era, wrong kitchen, wrong everything.
Dinah's Jacob's daughter, another Genesis name. Ruth 1:4 says Ruth. Dinah's story is a whole different tragedy. The Bible's got no shortage of hard stories, but this one's about Ruth.

Ruth 1:5 says it straight: both Mahlon and Chilion died. Naomi loses her husband, then ten years later loses both sons. That's three funerals. I think this one hurts, friend. That's a lot of grief for one person to carry.

explanations.answer: Her house in Moab burns down
explanations.explanation: No fire in the text. Ruth 1:5 says both her sons die. The Bible doesn't mention her house at all. Sometimes the plainest answer is the hardest one.

explanations.answer: She falls sick and loses her sight
explanations.explanation: Nothing about sickness or blindness here. Ruth 1:5 says both sons die. Naomi's affliction is loss, not illness. The text gives us what happened, not what we might expect.

Ruth 1:6 says the LORD attended to His people by providing them with food. That's why Naomi's heading back. The famine's over, the ovens are warm again, and Bethlehem's got bread. The name Bethlehem even means 'house of bread.' Fitting, isn't it?

No king yet. Ruth 1:6 says food. Israel's still in the judges period, which the first verse told us. No monarchy for a while. Saul and David are coming, but not now. Naomi's going back because there's bread, not because there's a crown.
No battle mentioned. Ruth 1:6 says food. The LORD provided food, not military victory. Sometimes the miracle is just bread on the table. I've baked enough to know that's no small thing.

explanations.answer: Go back to their mothers' homes
explanations.explanation: Ruth 1:8 has Naomi saying exactly that: 'Go back, each of you to your mother's home.' She's releasing them from obligation. No hard feelings, no guilt trip. Just go, find rest, start again. That's a selfless send-off if I've ever seen one.

explanations.answer: Walk faster to beat the dark
explanations.explanation: Nothing about walking faster or the dark. Ruth 1:8 says go back to your mother's home. Naomi's not worried about travel time. She's trying to get them to turn around entirely.

explanations.answer: Stay close to her the whole way
explanations.explanation: Opposite of what she says. Ruth 1:8 says go back, not stay close. Naomi's pushing them away, not pulling them in. She's got her reasons, and she lays them out next.

True. Ruth 1:9 says Naomi prays that the LORD enable each of them to find rest in the home of a new husband. She's blessing their future marriages. That's a mother-in-law who wants her daughters-in-law to be happy, even if it means never seeing them again.

Nope, it's true. Ruth 1:9 says exactly that: rest in the home of a new husband. Naomi's send-off is all about their future. She's not asking them to stay single and serve her. She wants them to find new lives.

explanations.answer: We will return with you to your people
explanations.explanation: Ruth 1:10 says it: 'Surely we will return with you to your people.' Both daughters-in-law say it together at first. They're not ready to leave her. Grief binds people sometimes, and loyalty runs deep.

explanations.answer: We will stay in Moab and wait for you
explanations.explanation: They don't offer to wait. Ruth 1:10 says they'll return with her. Staying in Moab would mean separating, and that's not what they want. Not yet, anyway.

explanations.answer: We will come visit you in Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: No visit planned. Ruth 1:10 says return with you. They're talking about permanent relocation, not a holiday trip. This is all-in or nothing for them.

explanations.answer: Would you wait for them to grow up
explanations.explanation: Ruth 1:13 asks exactly that: 'Would you wait for them to grow up?' Naomi's pointing out the absurdity. Even if she remarried tonight and had sons, Orpah and Ruth would be old women by the time these imaginary boys were grown. The math doesn't work, and Naomi knows it.

explanations.answer: Would you raise them as your own
explanations.explanation: Not what she asks. Ruth 1:13 says wait for them to grow up. Naomi's talking about years of waiting, not adoption. She's being practical to the point of painful.

explanations.answer: Would you go ahead to Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: No, that's not the question. Ruth 1:13 says wait for them to grow up. Naomi's hypothetical is about waiting, not traveling ahead. She's trying to show them there's no future with her.

explanations.answer: The LORD's hand has turned against her
explanations.explanation: Ruth 1:13 says it: 'the hand of the LORD has gone out against me.' Naomi feels targeted by God Himself. That's not just grief talking. That's someone who believes God is active in her suffering. Heavy stuff, friend.

explanations.answer: The people of Judah have turned against her
explanations.explanation: No mention of Judah's people. Ruth 1:13 says the LORD's hand. Naomi blames God, not neighbors. She hasn't even seen Judah's people yet. She's still on the road from Moab.

explanations.answer: The people of Moab have turned against her
explanations.explanation: Nothing about Moabites turning on her. Ruth 1:13 says the LORD's hand. Her sons married Moabite women, lived there ten years. No hostility mentioned. Her pain is theological, not social.

True. Ruth 1:14 says Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye. That's the last we see of Orpah. She makes a hard choice, a reasonable choice, and she goes back to her people and her gods. The text doesn't judge her. Sometimes going home is the right thing to do.
It is true. Ruth 1:14 says Orpah kissed her goodbye. Orpah does leave, but she leaves with Naomi's blessing and a kiss. This isn't a betrayal. It's just a different path.

False, actually. Ruth 1:14 says Ruth clung to her. Ruth stays. That's the whole point. Orpah goes back, Ruth doesn't. If they both left, we wouldn't have a book of Ruth. We'd have a book of Naomi going home alone.
Right, it's false. Ruth 1:14 says Ruth clung to her. While Orpah kisses goodbye, Ruth holds on. That's the moment everything turns. One leaves, one stays, and the story follows the one who stays.

True. Ruth 1:15 says Naomi tells Ruth, 'your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods; follow her back home.' Naomi's still pushing. She uses Orpah's choice as an example. Go back to your gods, your people, your old life. It's practical advice, but Ruth's about to refuse it.
It is true. Ruth 1:15 has Naomi saying exactly that. Follow Orpah. Go back to your people and your gods. Naomi's not giving up on convincing her. She's trying every angle.

explanations.answer: Naomi's God will be her God
explanations.explanation: Ruth 1:16 says it: 'your God will be my God.' That's the big one, friend. Ruth's not just changing address. She's changing allegiance. Moab had gods. Chemosh was the main one. Ruth's leaving all that behind. She's choosing the LORD, and she's choosing Naomi. That's commitment on two levels.

explanations.answer: She will take care of Naomi's house
explanations.explanation: Nothing about a house. Ruth 1:16 says your God will be my God. Ruth's promise is spiritual and personal, not real estate. She's talking about identity, not property.

explanations.answer: She will learn all the ways of Judah
explanations.explanation: Not mentioned. Ruth 1:16 says your God will be my God. She might learn Judah's ways, but that's not what she promises. Her pledge is about people and God, not customs and traditions.

Ruth 1:17 says it: 'if anything but death separates you and me.' That's as final as it gets. Ruth's not leaving. The only thing that can split them up is the one thing nobody comes back from. That's the kind of loyalty that makes you stop and stare.

Distance won't do it. Ruth 1:17 says death. Ruth's already walking distance. She's leaving Moab for Bethlehem. Distance is happening right now, and she's choosing it. She's saying even that won't separate them.

Not marriage. Ruth 1:17 says death. Naomi's whole point was that marriage would separate them. Ruth's saying no, only death. She's rejecting Naomi's logic entirely. Marriage won't split them. Nothing will.

explanations.answer: She stops trying to persuade her
explanations.explanation: Ruth 1:18 says it: 'she stopped trying to persuade her.' Naomi finally gets it. Ruth's not budging. When someone makes that kind of promise, you either accept it or waste more breath. Naomi accepts it. The arguing ends. The journey continues.

explanations.answer: She sends her back after Orpah
explanations.explanation: No more sending. Ruth 1:18 says she stopped trying to persuade her. Naomi's done pushing. Ruth's staying, and Naomi knows it. No more Orpah examples, no more practical objections.

explanations.answer: She tells her to wait in Moab
explanations.explanation: No waiting. Ruth 1:18 says she stopped trying to persuade her. They're going together. No delays, no conditions. Ruth's promise worked. Naomi relents.

Ruth 1:19 says the women exclaimed, 'Can this be Naomi?' They're shocked. Naomi left with a husband and two sons. She comes back with a foreign daughter-in-law and empty hands. Ten years and tragedy changes a person. The town barely recognizes her.
Not what they say. Ruth 1:19 says 'Can this be Naomi?' They're reacting to her appearance, not asking about Elimelech. Though if they did ask, the answer would break the moment even more.

They recognize her, barely. Ruth 1:19 says 'Can this be Naomi?' They're questioning if it's her, not assuming she's a stranger. Naomi's changed enough to make them doubt, but not so much they don't know who they're doubting about.

Ruth 1:20 says it: 'Call me Mara.' Naomi means 'pleasant.' Mara means 'bitter.' She's renaming herself based on what she feels the Almighty has done to her. That's a hard rename, friend. Like if I started calling myself 'Burnt Batch' because one tray came out wrong. Only her tray was her whole life.

Hannah's a different Bible woman, Samuel's mother from 1 Samuel. Ruth 1:20 says Mara. Hannah's story is later, and it's about prayer for a child. Naomi's story is about losing children. Different names, different pain.
Leah's Jacob's first wife from Genesis. Ruth 1:20 says Mara. Leah had her own troubles, but she's not in this story. Wrong book, wrong era, wrong kitchen.

False, actually. Ruth 1:21 says the opposite: 'I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty.' Naomi's reversing it. She left with family, she returns alone. That's the bitterness. That's the Mara.

Right, it's false. Ruth 1:21 says 'I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty.' She didn't leave empty and come back full. She left full and came back empty. That's her whole complaint. The Almighty has dealt bitterly with her.

Ruth 1:22 says barley. Not wheat, not olives. Barley. That's important, friend. Barley harvest comes first, early spring. Wheat's later. The barley harvest sets up what happens next, and trust me, you want to see what happens next. This story's got more baking to do.
Wheat's wrong. Ruth 1:22 says barley. Wheat harvest comes later in the year. The Bible specifies barley for a reason. Timing matters in this story, and barley's the right time.
Olives aren't harvested like grain. Ruth 1:22 says barley. Olives are picked, not reaped. Wrong crop, wrong season, wrong everything. This is grain country, and barley's the grain in season.
